ch26.title: Teaching About Prayer
ch26.b001: The Slopes of Mount Gilboa, September A.D. 27
ch26.b002: September and October were spent in retirement at a secluded camp on the slopes of Mount Gilboa, on the borders of Samaria and the Decapolis. There were good reasons for withdrawing. The religious rulers at Jerusalem were very antagonistic. Herod Antipas still held John in prison, fearing either to release him or to execute him, and he suspected that John and Jesus were in some way associated. And between the leaders of John’s disciples and the apostles of Jesus there was a slowly growing tension that worsened as the number of believers increased. Jesus told the twelve plainly that they were in retirement for three reasons: to confirm their understanding of, and faith in, the gospel of the kingdom; to allow the opposition in Judea and Galilee to quiet down; and to await the fate of John the Baptist.
ch26.b003: Jesus knew that the days of preliminary work were about over, and that the next move would begin the full and final effort of his life on earth. He did not wish that beginning to be in any way trying or embarrassing to John. So he rehearsed his apostles. He told them much about his early life and his experiences on Mount Hermon, and something of what had happened in the hills during the forty days after his baptism, and he charged them to tell no man of these things until after he had returned to the Father.
ch26.b004: During those September weeks they rested, recounted their experiences since he first called them, and tried earnestly to fit together all he had taught them. They sensed that this would be their last long rest, and that their next public effort would mark the beginning of the final proclamation of the kingdom. Yet they had little settled idea of what the kingdom would be. John and Andrew thought it had already come; Peter and James believed it was yet to come; Nathaniel and Thomas frankly confessed they were puzzled; Matthew, Philip, and Simon Zelotes were uncertain and confused; the twins were blissfully ignorant of the controversy; and Judas Iscariot was silent and noncommittal. Much of the time Jesus was alone on the mountain near the camp, in personal communion with his Father. And throughout the month the central theme of their talks was prayer and worship.
ch26.b006: John had taught his disciples a prayer, and all great teachers had formulated prayers for their pupils; the Jewish teachers had some twenty-five or thirty set prayers recited in the synagogues and even on street corners. But the apostles perceived early that their Master did not fully approve of uttering set and formal prayers. Jesus was particularly averse to praying in public, and up to this time the twelve had heard him pray only a few times, though they had seen him spend entire nights in prayer. They were hard pressed to know what to say when the multitudes asked to be taught to pray as John had taught his disciples. So one afternoon in the third week on Gilboa, Thomas made the request: “⟦Q 144:1.9⟧Master, teach us how to pray.⟦/Q⟧”
ch26.b007: Jesus first reminded them of John’s prayer: “⟦Q 144:2.1⟧O Father, cleanse us from sin, show us your glory, reveal your love, and let your spirit sanctify our hearts forevermore, Amen!⟦/Q⟧” John had taught it so they might have something to teach the multitude, not as the expression of their own souls. “⟦Q 144:2.2,144:2.3⟧Prayer is entirely a personal and spontaneous expression of the attitude of the soul toward the spirit; prayer should be the communion of sonship and the expression of fellowship. … Prayer is the breath of the soul and should lead you to be persistent in your attempt to ascertain the Father’s will.⟦/Q⟧”
ch26.b008: Then he told of a man who went to his neighbor at midnight to borrow three loaves for a friend who had come to him on a journey. The neighbor answered that the door was shut and the children in bed, yet because the man persisted, he rose at last and gave him all he needed. If persistence wins favors even from mortal men, how much more will persistence in the spirit win the bread of life from the willing hands of the Father. “⟦Q 144:2.3⟧Again I say to you: Ask and it shall be given you; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you.⟦/Q⟧” What father would give his child a stone when he needed a loaf, or a watersnake when he needed a fish? “⟦Q 144:2.4⟧If you, then, being mortal and finite, know how to answer prayer and give good and appropriate gifts to your children, how much more shall your heavenly Father give the spirit and many additional blessings to those who ask him?⟦/Q⟧”
ch26.b009: He told also of an unjust judge who feared neither God nor man, and of a needy widow who came to him again and again until he vindicated her lest she wear him out. But he warned them not to misunderstand. These stories were told to encourage them to persist in prayer, not to suggest that their petitions would change the just and righteous Father above. “⟦Q 144:2.5⟧Your persistence, however, is not to win favor with God but to change your earth attitude and to enlarge your soul’s capacity for spirit receptivity.⟦/Q⟧”
ch26.b010: The Prayer of the Nazareth Home
ch26.b011: Still the apostles were not satisfied. James Zebedee said: “⟦Q 144:3.1⟧Very good, Master, but we do not desire a form of prayer for ourselves so much as for the newer believers who so frequently beseech us, ‘Teach us how acceptably to pray to the Father in heaven.’⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 144:3.2⟧If, then, you still desire such a prayer, I would present the one which I taught my brothers and sisters in Nazareth.⟦/Q⟧”

ch26.b013.en: Our Father who is in heaven,

ch26.b015.en: Your kingdom come; your will be done

ch26.b016.en: On earth as it is in heaven.

ch26.b017.en: Give us this day our bread for tomorrow;

ch26.b018.en: Refresh our souls with the water of life.

ch26.b019.en: And forgive us every one our debts

ch26.b020.en: As we also have forgiven our debtors.

ch26.b021.en: Save us in temptation, deliver us from evil,

ch26.b022.en: And increasingly make us perfect like yourself.

ch26.b023: It was the prayer of the family, given in the collective form in which they had prayed it together in the Nazareth home. Jesus never taught a formal personal prayer, only group, family, or social petitions, and he never volunteered even these. For their own praying he taught the twelve always to pray in secret, to go off by themselves amid the quiet surroundings of nature, or to go into their rooms and shut the doors.
ch26.b024: Effective prayer, he taught, must be unselfish, not alone for oneself; believing, according to faith; sincere, honest of heart; intelligent, according to light; and trustful, in submission to the Father’s all-wise will. When he spent whole nights on the mountain, it was mainly for his disciples, particularly the twelve, that he prayed; for himself he prayed very little. Peter, James, and John, who so often went with him on those long vigils, never heard him pray, because practically all his praying was done silently, in the spirit and in the heart. In the time that remained he brought to their notice several other forms of prayer, many of them from other inhabited worlds, though he did not tell them so; but these “parable prayers” he enjoined them not to teach to the multitudes. Of all the apostles, Peter and James came nearest to comprehending his teaching about prayer and worship.
ch26.b026: Around the first of October, Philip and some of the others were buying food in a near-by village when they met some of the apostles of John the Baptist, for John, at Abner’s urging, had recently appointed twelve of his leaders as apostles after the example of Jesus. Out of that chance meeting in the market place came a three weeks’ conference at the Gilboa camp. The twenty-four men met three times a day, six days a week, with Andrew and Abner presiding in turn.
ch26.b027: They wanted the Master to preside over their deliberations, but he steadfastly refused, though he spoke to them on three occasions, on sympathy, co-operation, and tolerance. When they brought him their troubles, he would say: “⟦Q 144:6.3⟧I am concerned only with your personal and purely religious problems. I am the representative of the Father to the individual, not to the group.⟦/Q⟧” The socializing of religion they must settle by their own decisions; but if they all agreed, he pledged in advance his full approval and hearty co-operation. “⟦Q 144:6.3⟧And now, in order to leave you unhampered in your deliberations, I am leaving you for two weeks. Be not anxious about me, for I will return to you. I will be about my Father’s business, for we have other realms besides this one.⟦/Q⟧” He went down the mountainside, and for two full weeks they did not see him. They never knew where he went or what he did.
ch26.b028: At first they were so disconcerted by his absence that they could hardly settle to work, but within a week they were deep in their discussions. The first thing they agreed upon, unanimously, was that both groups would teach believers the prayer Jesus had just given. The most serious problem was baptism, all the harder because Jesus would make no pronouncement on it. They finally agreed that as long as John lived, only John’s apostles would baptize, and Jesus’ apostles would instruct the new disciples. If John died, his apostles would come under the direction of Jesus, and Jesus’ apostles would begin to baptize with water as the emblem of the baptism of the divine Spirit. John’s apostles would go on preaching, “Repent and be baptized,” and Jesus’ apostles, “Believe and be baptized.” It was the first attempt of Jesus’ followers to organize and socialize their religion, and in those two weeks they learned to differ, to debate, to contend, to pray, and to compromise. On the afternoon of their final session Jesus returned, listened to their decisions, and said: “⟦Q 144:6.12⟧These, then, are your conclusions, and I shall help you each to carry out the spirit of your united decisions.⟦/Q⟧”
ch26.b030: The Gilboa camp was broken up on November 2, A.D. 27. Through November and December Jesus and the twenty-four worked quietly in the Greek cities of the Decapolis, chiefly Scythopolis, Gerasa, Abila, and Gadara, going out in pairs, one of Jesus’ apostles with one of John’s; John’s apostle baptized and Jesus’ apostle instructed. John’s men came to understand why Jesus did not visit John in prison or try to free him, but they never could understand why he did no marvelous works and refused to show outward signs of his authority. Before Gilboa they had believed in him mostly because of John’s testimony; now they were beginning to believe because of their own contact with the Master.
ch26.b031: In the latter part of December they moved to a camp near Pella. One afternoon, as Jesus was teaching the multitude, some of John’s special friends interrupted him with the last message he would ever have from the Baptist, who had now been in prison a year and a half: “⟦Q 144:8.2⟧John the Baptist has sent us to ask—are you truly the Deliverer, or shall we look for another?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus paused and said: “⟦Q 144:8.3⟧Go back and tell John that he is not forgotten. Tell him what you have seen and heard, that the poor have good tidings preached to them.⟦/Q⟧”
ch26.b032: Then he turned to the crowd. They must not think that John doubted the gospel; he asked only to assure his disciples. What had they gone out to see when they heard John preach, a reed shaken with the wind, a man clothed in soft raiment? A prophet, and much more than a prophet. “⟦Q 144:8.4⟧Verily, verily, I say to you, among those born of women there has not arisen a greater than John the Baptist; yet he who is but small in the kingdom of heaven is greater because he has been born of the spirit and knows that he has become a son of God.⟦/Q⟧” From that day John’s apostles were firmly knit to Jesus. The messengers went back to Machaerus, and John was greatly comforted. And Jesus went on teaching that afternoon: “⟦Q 144:8.8⟧Come, therefore, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and you shall find rest for your souls.⟦/Q⟧”
ch26.b034: On the evening of January 10, A.D. 28, John the Baptist was executed at Machaerus by order of Herod Antipas. A few of his disciples obtained his body and later buried it at Sebaste, the home of Abner. On January 12 they came north to the camp near Pella and told Jesus. When he heard their report, he dismissed the multitude and called the twenty-four together. “⟦Q 144:9.1⟧John is dead. Herod has beheaded him. Tonight go into joint council and arrange your affairs accordingly. There shall be delay no longer. The hour has come to proclaim the kingdom openly and with power. Tomorrow we go into Galilee.⟦/Q⟧”
ch26.b035: Early on the morning of January 13, A.D. 28, Jesus and the apostles, with some twenty-five disciples, set out for Capernaum, and that night they lodged in the house of Zebedee.
ch27.title: Healing at Sundown
ch27.b002: On the evening of Tuesday, January 13, Jesus and the apostles reached Capernaum and, as usual, made their headquarters at the home of Zebedee in Bethsaida. Now that John the Baptist had been sent to his death, Jesus prepared to launch out on the first open and public preaching tour of Galilee. The news of his return spread rapidly through the city, and early the next day Mary his mother hastened away to Nazareth to visit her son Joseph. From Wednesday through Friday Jesus stayed at Zebedee’s house instructing the apostles for the coming tour and receiving earnest inquirers, and through Andrew he arranged to speak in the synagogue on the coming Sabbath.
ch27.b003: Late on Friday evening his baby sister, Ruth, secretly came to see him. They spent almost an hour together in a boat anchored a short distance from the shore. No one but John Zebedee ever knew of this visit, and he was admonished to tell no man. Ruth was the only member of the family who consistently and unwaveringly believed in the divinity of his earth mission, from her earliest spiritual consciousness through his ministry, death, resurrection, and ascension. Throughout the trying ordeal of his trial, rejection, and crucifixion, she was his chief comfort as regards his earth family.
ch27.b005: On that same Friday morning, as Jesus taught by the seaside, the people pressed him so close to the water’s edge that he signaled to some fishermen in a near-by boat to come to his rescue. The boat was named “Simon.” It was Simon Peter’s former fishing vessel and had been built by Jesus’ own hands. That morning David Zebedee and two associates were using it; they had just come in from a fruitless night on the lake and were cleaning and mending their nets. Jesus stepped into the boat and went on teaching the multitude for more than two hours.
ch27.b006: When he had finished, he said to David: “⟦Q 145:1.2⟧As you were delayed by coming to my help, now let me work with you. Let us go fishing; put out into yonder deep and let down your nets for a draught.⟦/Q⟧” One of David’s assistants, a man named Simon, answered: “⟦Q 145:1.2⟧Master, it is useless. We toiled all night and took nothing; however, at your bidding we will put out and let down the nets.⟦/Q⟧” They let down the nets where Jesus showed them and enclosed such a multitude of fish that they feared the nets would break; they filled all three boats almost to sinking. Then this Simon fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, “⟦Q 145:1.2⟧Depart from me, Master, for I am a sinful man.⟦/Q⟧” From that day David Zebedee, Simon, and their associates forsook their nets and followed Jesus. Yet this was in no sense a miraculous draught of fishes. Jesus was an experienced fisherman who knew the habits of the fish in the Sea of Galilee; he simply directed them to the place where the fish were usually found at that time of day. His followers always regarded it as a miracle.
ch27.b008: At the afternoon service on the Sabbath, Jesus preached on “⟦Q 145:2.1⟧The Will of the Father in Heaven.⟦/Q⟧” For his texts he read from Exodus and from Isaiah, and his sermon sought to make clear that religion is a personal experience. “⟦Q 145:2.4⟧No longer must you approach the Father in heaven as a child of Israel but as a child of God. As a group, you are indeed the children of Israel, but as individuals, each one of you is a child of God. … All these generations have you had a national or racial religion; now have I come to give you a personal religion.⟦/Q⟧” The people of Capernaum knew his teaching, yet they were astonished, for he taught as one having authority and not as the scribes. And they could not forget the closing words of that sermon: “⟦Q 145:3.4⟧Hate is the shadow of fear; revenge the mask of cowardice,⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 145:3.4⟧Man is the son of God, not a child of the devil.⟦/Q⟧”
ch27.b009: Just as he finished, a young man in the congregation who had been much agitated by his words was seized with a violent epileptic attack and cried out. Coming to himself, he spoke as in a dream: “⟦Q 145:2.12⟧What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? You are the holy one of God; have you come to destroy us?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus bade the people be quiet and, taking the young man by the hand, said, “Come out of it”—and he was immediately awakened. He was not possessed of a demon; he suffered from ordinary epilepsy and had been taught that his affliction came from an evil spirit. The people believed that Jesus had cast a demon out of him, and on the Sabbath the rumor spread swiftly through Capernaum and the villages around it.
ch27.b010: On the way back from the synagogue they stopped at Peter’s house near by, for Peter’s mother-in-law, Amatha, had been sick for several days with malarial fever. It chanced that just as Jesus stood over her, holding her hand, smoothing her brow, and speaking words of comfort, the fever left her. Recalling the water and the wine at Cana, some of the apostles seized on this coincidence as another miracle and rushed out to spread the news through the city. But she was not truly healed until several hours later, after sundown.
ch27.b012: By the time Jesus and the apostles sat down to their evening meal, all Capernaum was agog over these reputed healings, and everyone who was sick or afflicted prepared to go to Jesus the moment the Sabbath ended, for according to Jewish teaching it was not permissible even to go in quest of health during the sacred hours. As soon as the sun sank beneath the horizon, scores of afflicted men, women, and children began to make their way toward the Zebedee home. One man started out with his paralyzed daughter as soon as the sun sank behind his neighbor’s house.
ch27.b013: Soon after sunset, while they still lingered at table, Peter’s wife heard voices in the front yard. At the door she saw a great company of sick folk gathering, and the road from Capernaum crowded with others coming, and she told her husband, who told Jesus. When the Master stepped out of the front entrance, he looked upon almost one thousand human beings in the dusk, the sick and ailing and those who had come helping their loved ones. The sight of these suffering mortals peculiarly touched his human heart and challenged the divine mercy of the Creator Son. Yet he knew that he could never build an enduring spiritual movement upon purely material wonders, and not since Cana had the supernatural attended his teaching.
ch27.b014: A voice from the yard cried out: “⟦Q 145:3.8⟧Master, speak the word, restore our health, heal our diseases, and save our souls.⟦/Q⟧” At once the vast retinue of seraphim, physical controllers, Life Carriers, and midwayers that always attended him made ready to act should their Sovereign give the signal. It was one of those moments when divine wisdom and human compassion were so interlocked that the Son of Man sought refuge in his Father’s will. When Peter implored him to heed their cry, Jesus looked down upon the afflicted throng and said: “⟦Q 145:3.9⟧I have come into the world to reveal the Father and establish his kingdom. For this purpose have I lived my life to this hour. If, therefore, it should be the will of Him who sent me and not inconsistent with my dedication to the proclamation of the gospel of the kingdom of heaven, I would desire to see my children made whole—and—⟦/Q⟧” but his further words were lost in the tumult.
ch27.b015: He had passed the decision to his Father, and evidently the Father’s will interposed no objection. Scarcely had he spoken when the celestial hosts serving under his Personalized Thought Adjuster descended into the midst of that motley throng, and in a moment of time 683 men, women, and children were made whole of all their physical diseases. Such a scene was never witnessed on earth before that day, nor since. And of all who were astonished, Jesus himself was the most surprised. With his human sympathies focused on the suffering before him, he had not borne in mind the warnings of his Adjuster that the time element of a Creator Son’s prerogatives could not always be limited. He desired to see them whole if the Father’s will would not be violated; the Adjuster instantly ruled that it would not, and so the creative act was. Never again in his earth life did such a mass healing take place.
ch27.b017: All that evening a rejoicing throng overran Zebedee’s home, and the apostles were keyed up to the highest pitch of enthusiasm. Never before or after did their hopes surge so high; they thought they saw the fulfillment of his word that the kingdom would be proclaimed in power. But when they looked for Jesus, he could not be found. The healed lingered late, hoping to thank him. When at last he returned, nearly all had gone home, and he refused the congratulations of the twelve, saying only: “⟦Q 145:4.2⟧Rejoice not that my Father is powerful to heal the body, but rather that he is mighty to save the soul. Let us go to our rest, for tomorrow we must be about the Father’s business.⟦/Q⟧” Again twelve perplexed and disappointed men went to their rest, and few of them, except the twins, slept much. As they looked into each other’s eyes, there was but one thought: “⟦Q 145:4.3⟧We cannot understand him. What does all this mean?⟦/Q⟧”
ch27.b018: Neither did Jesus sleep much. He saw the danger of being compelled to devote so much time to the sick that his mission of establishing the spiritual kingdom in men’s hearts would be crowded aside. Long before daybreak on Sunday he went out alone into the hills to pray for wisdom and judgment. Peter roused James and John, and after more than an hour’s search they found him. For more than four hours he tried to explain why the kingdom could not be built upon wonder-working and physical healing, but they could not comprehend his teaching.
ch27.b019: Meanwhile new crowds had gathered at Zebedee’s house, clamoring to see him, and Andrew came to beg him to return and minister to them. Jesus asked whether they came for spiritual truth or for the healing of their bodies. “⟦Q 145:5.7⟧No, Andrew, I will not return with you. Go and tell the people to believe in that which we have taught them and to rejoice in the liberty of the sons of God, and make ready for our departure for the other cities of Galilee.⟦/Q⟧” Sorrowfully the apostles went back and dismissed the multitude. Peter reckoned that no fewer than a thousand believers could have been baptized. There was a silence, and then Thomas said: “⟦Q 145:5.10⟧Let’s go! The Master has spoken. No matter if we cannot fully comprehend the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, of one thing we are certain: We follow a teacher who seeks no glory for himself.⟦/Q⟧” On the afternoon of Sunday, January 18, A.D. 28, they set out for Rimmon on their first public preaching tour of Galilee. Shortly after they had gone, his brothers James and Jude came to Zebedee’s house to see him.
ch28.title: The Galilean Preaching Tour
ch28.b002: On Sunday, January 18, A.D. 28, Jesus and the twelve set out from Capernaum, and with them went the former apostles of John. It was the beginning of the first public preaching tour of Galilee. For about two months the company moved from town to town through the winter hills—Rimmon, Jotapata, Ramah, Zebulun, Iron, Gischala, Chorazin, Madon, Cana, Nain, and Endor. For the first time Jesus permitted his associates to preach without restraint. He cautioned them on only three occasions: to remain away from Nazareth, and to be discreet when passing through Capernaum and Tiberias. The apostles threw themselves into the work of preaching, ministering to the sick, and baptizing believers with great earnestness and joy.
ch28.b003: The first stop, the small city of Rimmon, had once been dedicated to Ramman, a Babylonian god of the air. Many of the older Babylonian and later Zoroastrian teachings still lingered in the beliefs of its people, and so Jesus and the twenty-four spent much of their time making plain the difference between these older beliefs and the new gospel of the kingdom. Here Peter preached one of the great sermons of his early career, on “Aaron and the Golden Calf.” Many became believers, though it is difficult to bring nature worshipers into the full fellowship of a spiritual ideal within a single lifetime. Yet it was at Rimmon that Todan first heard the gospel of the kingdom, and he later carried this message into Mesopotamia and far beyond, among the first to preach the good news to those who dwelt beyond the Euphrates.
ch28.b005: The common people of Jotapata heard Jesus and his apostles gladly, and many accepted the gospel. But what made this small town memorable was an evening discourse on the second night of their stay. Nathaniel was confused in his mind about the Master’s teachings concerning prayer, thanksgiving, and worship, and when he asked his question, Jesus gathered the twenty-four about him in the lamplight and spoke at great length.
ch28.b006: The conscious and persistent regard for iniquity in the heart, he said, gradually destroys the prayer connection between the soul and its Maker. The Father in heaven has forgiven us even before we think to ask, yet such forgiveness is not available in our personal religious experience until we forgive our fellow men. They who would receive mercy must show mercy. A thoroughly selfish soul cannot pray in the true sense of the word. Prayer does not change the divine attitude toward man, but it does change man’s attitude toward the changeless Father. He bade them avoid praying much for themselves and pray more for the spiritual progress of their brethren. When they prayed for the sick, they must not expect their petitions to take the place of loving and intelligent ministry to the afflicted. They were to pray for families and friends, but especially for those who cursed them, and to make loving petitions for those who persecuted them. And there is but one form of prayer appropriate for all God’s children: “Nevertheless, your will be done.”
ch28.b007: Jesus deplored that so little of the spirit of thanksgiving was to be found in the prayers and worship of his followers, and he taught them that, when they had made their prayers to the Father, they should remain for a time in silent receptivity, to afford the indwelling spirit the better opportunity to speak to the listening soul. Worship, he taught, makes one increasingly like the being who is worshiped. It is a transforming experience whereby the finite gradually approaches and at last attains the presence of the Infinite. Not many of them could fully encompass his teaching that night.
ch28.b009: At Ramah Jesus had a memorable discussion with an aged Greek philosopher who taught that science and philosophy were sufficient to satisfy the needs of human experience. The Master listened with patience and sympathy, allowing the truth of many things the old man said. But when the Greek was through, Jesus pointed out that he had failed to explain the “whence, why, and whither” of human existence. “⟦Q 146:3.1⟧Where you leave off, we begin,⟦/Q⟧” he said. For more than an hour Jesus taught him the saving truths of the gospel, and the old philosopher, being sincerely honest of heart, quickly believed.
ch28.b010: When the apostles were disconcerted by his open assent to the Greek, Jesus said to them privately: “⟦Q 146:3.2⟧My children, marvel not that I was tolerant of the Greek’s philosophy. True and genuine inward certainty does not in the least fear outward analysis, nor does truth resent honest criticism. You should never forget that intolerance is the mask covering up the entertainment of secret doubts as to the trueness of one’s belief.⟦/Q⟧”
ch28.b011: On the second evening at Ramah, Thomas asked: “⟦Q 146:3.3⟧Master, how can a new believer in your teaching really know, really be certain, about the truth of this gospel of the kingdom?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered that such assurance “⟦Q 146:3.4⟧is wholly a matter of personal experience—faith in the word of truth.⟦/Q⟧” Though they could not observe the divine spirit at work in their minds, there was a practical way to discover how far they had yielded to its guidance, “⟦Q 146:3.6⟧and that is the degree of your love for your fellow men.⟦/Q⟧” Presently the Spirit of Truth would be poured out upon all flesh and would bear witness that they were in reality the sons of God. The Jewish teachings about the survival of the righteous had been confused and uncertain, and these definite words of assurance greatly cheered all who heard them.
ch28.b012: From this time each of Jesus’ apostles had one of John’s apostles as an associate; Abner was paired with Andrew. At Zebulun, among a people of mixed race, hardly Jew or gentile, few really believed.
ch28.b014: Iron, a town of extensive mineral mines, held something new for Jesus. Having never shared the life of the miner, while the apostles visited the homes and preached in the public places, he spent most of his days below ground, working in the mines beside the laborers.
ch28.b015: Late on the afternoon of the third day, as Jesus was returning from the mines, he chanced to pass through a narrow side street on the way to his lodging. As he drew near the squalid hovel of a certain leper, the man made bold to accost him and knelt before him, saying: “⟦Q 146:4.3⟧Lord, if only you would, you could make me clean. I have heard the message of your teachers, and I would enter the kingdom if I could be made clean.⟦/Q⟧” Lepers were forbidden even to attend the synagogue, and this man believed he could not enter the kingdom unless he was cured. When Jesus saw him in his affliction and heard his words of clinging faith, his human heart was touched, and the divine mind was moved with compassion. The man fell upon his face and worshiped. Then the Master stretched forth his hand and, touching him, said: “I will—be clean.” And immediately the leprosy was gone.
ch28.b016: Jesus lifted him to his feet and charged him: “⟦Q 146:4.4⟧See that you tell no man about your healing but rather go quietly about your business, showing yourself to the priest and offering those sacrifices commanded by Moses in testimony of your cleansing.⟦/Q⟧” But the man did not go to the priests. He went through the town telling everyone that Jesus had cured his leprosy, and since he was known to the whole village, all could see that he was clean. The sick thronged the Master so that he was forced to rise early the next day and leave. This was the first so-called miracle Jesus had intentionally and deliberately performed, and it was a case of real leprosy.
ch28.b017: From Iron they went to Gischala for two days, and then to Chorazin, where they spent almost a week. In no place had Jesus met with such a general rejection of his message. Passing quietly through Capernaum, they went on to Madon, where they fared little better. Most of the apostles blamed the Master’s refusal to let them speak of him as a healer. How they wished he would cleanse another leper, or in some other way so manifest his power as to attract the attention of the people! But the Master was unmoved by their earnest urging.
ch28.b019: The company was greatly cheered when Jesus announced, “Tomorrow we go to Cana.” He was well known there, and they were sure of a sympathetic hearing. On the third day there arrived a prominent citizen of Capernaum named Titus, a partial believer, whose son was critically ill. He found Jesus and besought him to hurry to Capernaum. While the apostles stood by in breathless expectancy, Jesus looked at the father and said: “⟦Q 146:5.2⟧How long shall I bear with you? The power of God is in your midst, but except you see signs and behold wonders, you refuse to believe.⟦/Q⟧” But the nobleman pleaded: “⟦Q 146:5.2⟧My Lord, I do believe, but come ere my child perishes, for when I left him he was even then at the point of death.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus bowed his head a moment in silent meditation, and then suddenly spoke: “⟦Q 146:5.2⟧Return to your home; your son will live.⟦/Q⟧” Titus believed and hastened home. On the way his servants met him, saying, “⟦Q 146:5.2⟧Rejoice, for your son is improved—he lives.⟦/Q⟧” When he asked at what hour the boy had begun to mend, they answered, “⟦Q 146:5.2⟧yesterday about the seventh hour the fever left him,⟦/Q⟧” and he recalled that it was the very hour when Jesus had spoken. Titus and all his household believed. Everyone regarded this as a miracle, but it was not a miracle of curing disease. It was a case of preknowledge concerning the course of natural law, such knowledge as Jesus frequently resorted to after his baptism.
ch28.b020: The townspeople, remembering the water and the wine, now brought their sick and even sent messengers asking for healing at a distance. When Jesus saw that the whole countryside was aroused, he said, “Let us go to Nain.”
ch28.b021: A great multitude of believers and curious people followed him, bent on beholding wonders. As Jesus and his apostles drew near the gate of Nain, they met a funeral procession bearing to the cemetery the only son of a widowed mother. She was much respected, and half the village walked behind the bier. When the procession came up to Jesus, the widow and her friends recognized him and besought him to bring her son back to life. Jesus stepped forward, raised the covering of the bier, and examined the boy. Discovering that the young man was not really dead, he perceived the tragedy his presence could avert, and he turned to the mother: “⟦Q 146:6.2⟧Weep not. Your son is not dead; he sleeps. He will be restored to you.⟦/Q⟧” Then, taking the young man by the hand, he said, “Awake and arise.” The youth sat up and began to speak.
ch28.b022: Jesus tried to calm the multitude and to explain that the lad had not been dead, that he had not brought him back from the grave, but it was useless. Not until long after nightfall could the frenzied throng be dispersed. Everyone insisted that the dead had been raised. The report went abroad through Galilee and into Judea, and once again besieged as a physician, Jesus left early the next morning for Endor. There, during a few days of rest, he told the apostles the story of King Saul and the witch of Endor. The spirits of departed human beings, he said, do not come back to communicate with their living fellows.
ch28.b024: The party returned to Capernaum on March 17 and spent two weeks at the Bethsaida headquarters. On the day before they made ready to go up to Jerusalem for the Passover, Mangus, a centurion of the Roman guard stationed at Capernaum, sent the rulers of the synagogue to Jesus on behalf of his faithful orderly, who lay at the point of death. The elders pleaded that this Roman loved their nation and had even built their synagogue. Jesus said, “I will go with you.” But before they reached the centurion’s yard, friends came out with his message: “⟦Q 147:1.2⟧Lord, trouble not yourself to enter my house, for I am not worthy that you should come under my roof.… But I know that you can speak the word where you stand and my servant will be healed.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus turned to those who followed him: “⟦Q 147:1.3⟧I marvel at the belief of the gentile. Verily, verily, I say to you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.⟦/Q⟧” From that hour the servant began to mend. Just what happened was never revealed; it is known only that the servant recovered completely.
ch28.b025: On March 30 they set out by the Jordan valley route and reached Bethany on April 2. To escape the crowds they pitched tents at Gethsemane as well, and this time Jesus enjoined them to do no public preaching, only private teaching. On the afternoon of the second Sabbath, John said to him, “⟦Q 147:3.1⟧Come with me, I would show you something,⟦/Q⟧” and led him out through one of the city gates to the pool of Bethesda. Under its five porches lay a multitude of sufferers. It was popularly believed that the first to enter the hot spring after its waters bubbled up would be healed. John hoped the sight would move the Master to a miracle that would astound all Jerusalem. “⟦Q 147:3.2⟧Master, see all of these suffering ones; is there nothing we can do for them?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 147:3.2⟧John, why would you tempt me to turn aside from the way I have chosen?… My son, I may not do that which you desire, but gather together these sick and afflicted that I may speak words of good cheer and eternal comfort to them.⟦/Q⟧” To the gathered sufferers he said: “⟦Q 147:3.3⟧You are all God’s children.… The bonds of time may seem to afflict you, but the God of eternity loves you.⟦/Q⟧” One man, for many years downcast and grievously afflicted by the infirmities of a troubled mind, rejoiced at these words, picked up his bed, and went home, though it was the Sabbath day. He had waited years for someone to help him, never thinking to help himself—and that was the one thing he had to do: take up his bed and walk.
ch28.b026: That same Sabbath evening, around the fire in Lazarus’s garden at Bethany, Nathaniel asked how the rule of doing to others as we would have them do to us could apply to a lustful man. Jesus explained six levels of meaning in that rule: the level of the flesh, of the feelings, of mind, of brotherly love, the moral level, and last and greatest, the spiritual level, which “⟦Q 147:4.9⟧impels us to recognize in this rule of life the divine command to treat all men as we conceive God would treat them.⟦/Q⟧”
ch28.b027: In the House of Simon the Pharisee
ch28.b028: Simon, an influential Pharisee of Jerusalem and a halfhearted believer, dared to invite Jesus, Peter, James, and John to a meal in his home. As was the custom, the doors were left open, and people from the street stood along the walls. Among them was a woman well known throughout Jerusalem as the former keeper of one of the high-class brothels hard by the temple court of the gentiles. On accepting the gospel she had closed her house and led most of its women to change their lives; yet she was still compelled to wear her hair down, the badge of harlotry. She had brought a large flask of perfumed anointing lotion, and standing behind Jesus as he reclined at meat, she anointed his feet, wet them with her tears of gratitude, wiped them with her hair, and went on weeping and kissing them.
ch28.b029: Simon said to himself: “⟦Q 147:5.4⟧This man, if he were a prophet, would have perceived who and what manner of woman this is who thus touches him; that she is a notorious sinner.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus, knowing his thoughts, told him of a moneylender who forgave two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii and the other fifty, and asked which would love him most. “⟦Q 147:5.4⟧He, I suppose, whom he forgave the most,⟦/Q⟧” Simon answered. Then Jesus pointed to the woman. Simon had given him no water for his feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for his head; this woman had washed his feet with tears, had not ceased to kiss them, and had anointed them with precious lotions. “⟦Q 147:5.4⟧And what is the meaning of all this? Simply that her many sins have been forgiven, and this has led her to love much.⟦/Q⟧” Taking her by the hand and lifting her up, he said, “⟦Q 147:5.4⟧Be not discouraged by the thoughtless and unkind attitude of your fellows; go on in the joy and liberty of the kingdom of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Then he dismissed her, saying, “⟦Q 147:5.5⟧Woman, go in peace; your faith has saved you.⟦/Q⟧”
ch28.b030: That evening, at the camp in Gethsemane, he spoke to the apostles of status and progress. “⟦Q 147:5.7⟧The important thing is not the rapidity of your progress but rather its certainty.… What you are becoming day by day is of infinitely more importance than what you are today.⟦/Q⟧” The woman, humanly speaking, was farther from God than Simon, but her soul was in progressive motion. “⟦Q 147:5.8⟧Better by far to have a small but living and growing faith than to be possessed of a great intellect with its dead stores of worldly wisdom and spiritual unbelief.⟦/Q⟧” Yet he warned them against presuming upon the Father’s love; the heavenly Father is not a lax or foolishly indulgent parent.
ch28.b032: The chief priests in Jerusalem had resolved that Jesus must be apprehended on a religious charge and tried by the Sanhedrin. A commission of six secret spies was appointed to follow him, and in the last week of April, under the pretense of desiring to become disciples, they attached themselves to the party of about thirty at Jericho. After three crowded days near the Jordan, the company set out early on Sabbath morning, the first day of May. The spies were sure they now had their first charge—Sabbath breaking—but before them all Jesus instructed Andrew to proceed only one thousand yards, the legal Sabbath day’s journey.
ch28.b033: They did not wait long. As the company passed along a narrow road between fields of ripening wheat, some of the hungry apostles plucked the grain and rubbed it in their hands to eat, as travelers customarily did. The spies rushed to Jesus in protest. He reminded them how David, when hungry, had eaten the showbread. “⟦Q 147:6.4⟧My good men, you do well to be zealous for the Sabbath, but you would do better to guard the health and well-being of your fellows. I declare that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath. And if you are here present with us to watch my words, then will I openly proclaim that the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.⟦/Q⟧” For the rest of the day the Pharisees dared not ask any more questions.
ch28.b034: On Monday, May 3, Jesus and the twelve reached Bethsaida by boat from Tarichea. The next evening the leader of the spies asked why his disciples did not fast. “⟦Q 147:7.2⟧Do the sons of the bridechamber fast while the bridegroom is with them?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered, and spoke of new cloth on an old garment and new wine in fresh wine skins. Yet, he added, “⟦Q 147:7.3⟧That which is old and also true must abide.⟦/Q⟧” Long after the usual listeners had gone, he taught the apostles from Isaiah of the fast God chooses—to loose the bonds of wickedness, to let the oppressed go free, to share bread with the hungry. His last words, spoken after two o’clock in the morning, were: “⟦Q 147:8.5⟧Grow in grace by means of that living faith which grasps the fact that you are the sons of God while at the same time it recognizes every man as a brother.⟦/Q⟧”
